steps.observation: Work on this for 10 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptual overview of a transformer neural network:

1. Inputs as vectors  
   • Every word (or image patch, audio frame, etc.) is turned into a fixed-length vector called an embedding.  
   • A position encoding is added to each vector so the model knows the order of the inputs.

2. Self-attention layers  
   • For each position, the model forms three short vectors: Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V).  
   • A word’s Query asks, “Which other words matter to me?”  
   • By dot-producting Q with all Ks, the model gets relevance scores, then softmax-normalizes them into weights.  
   • It uses those weights to blend the corresponding Value vectors into a new representation of the word that now “knows” about the whole context.  
   • Doing this in parallel for multiple, independent “heads” lets the model capture different kinds of relationships (syntax, co-reference, etc.).

3. Feed-forward sublayer  
   • After attention, each position’s vector passes through an independent small neural network (two linear layers with a non-linearity in between) to refine the representation.

4. Add & Norm  
   • Each sublayer (attention or feed-forward) is wrapped with residual connections (“add the input back in”) followed by layer normalization.  
   • This stabilizes training and preserves information.

5. Stacking layers  
   • A transformer block (attention + feed-forward) is stacked many times (e.g., 6–96 layers).  
   • Deeper layers allow progressively richer abstractions.

6. Output heads  
   • For language modeling, the final vectors are projected to vocabulary logits to predict the next token.  
   • For tasks like translation or summarization, an additional decoder (another stack of blocks) consumes the encoder’s outputs and generates text autoregressively.

Key ideas in plain words:

• Attention as information routing: Each element can look at every other element and decide whom to listen to, instead of relying on fixed-width windows like RNNs/CNNs.  
• Parallelism: Because attention looks at all positions at once, transformers train efficiently on GPUs.  
• Flexibility: The same architecture works for text, images, audio, and more by just changing the embeddings and output heads.  
• Scalability: Performance keeps improving as you add layers, heads, and parameters, which is why very large transformers power state-of-the-art models today.
